articles.title: Disneyland tears down historic 71-year-old ticket booths amid major expansion plans, including Porto’s Bakery, new Coco and Avatar experiences and Avengers Campus attractions in 2028
articles.summary: Disneyland has demolished the final two ticket booths on the eastern side of its main entrance in Anaheim, California, removing structures that had stood
articles.body: Disneyland has demolished the final two ticket booths on the eastern side of its main entrance in Anaheim, California, removing structures that had stood for 71 years as the theme park prepares for a major expansion. The demolition marks another change to the historic entrance area as Disney advances its Disneyland Forward initiative, which includes new infrastructure, dining options and attractions.The final two ticket booths on the eastern side of the entrance to the “Happiest Place on Earth” have been bulldozed, leaving behind piles of wood and concrete. According to Inside the Magic, aerial images captured from the Disneyland monorail and shared on social media on Tuesday showed the demolished structures behind construction walls in the Esplanade area.The demolition follows the removal of four other ticket booths earlier this year between Disneyland and Disney California Adventure Park. With the latest structures gone, visitors who prefer purchasing tickets in person will have two remaining booths on the western side of the Esplanade.The booths had been a familiar feature of the resort for decades, making their removal another visible sign of the changes underway at the popular Southern California destination.Disneyland expansion includes new entrance experienceThe demolition comes as Disney moves ahead with Disneyland Forward, an ambitious expansion initiative announced in 2024 that aims to transform the resort and improve how visitors arrive, move around and access its attractions.According to Disney’s latest project update, the plans include a new pedestrian bridge over Harbor Boulevard, leading to an “all-new esplanade arrival experience”.The proposal also includes a new parking structure and transportation hub designed to accommodate 6,000 vehicles. Plans call for dedicated shuttle and rideshare areas, security screening and access for traffic from Disney Way, with the aim of improving parking and traffic flow throughout the resort.The changes are expected to reshape parts of the surrounding area as Disneyland continues developing its long-term plans for the property.Porto’s Bakery and Cafe planned for Downtown DisneyAnother major addition planned for the resort is a new Porto’s Bakery and Cafe location in the Downtown Disney District, as reported by WDW News Today.The popular Los Angeles-area bakery was founded by Cuban immigrants, who opened their first shop in Echo Park in the 1970s. The business has since expanded to six locations, with the Disneyland resort set to become home to its seventh.Porto’s shared an artist’s rendering of the proposed location on Instagram last year, showing a spacious, two-storey design with outdoor seating.“Serving up a fresh new view of what’s to come... Construction is officially underway for the all-new Porto’s Bakery & Cafe coming to Downtown Disney District!” the bakery said in its post.The planned outlet is expected to add another dining option for visitors exploring Downtown Disney, the shopping and entertainment district outside the theme parks.Avengers Campus, Coco and Avatar attractions in the pipelineDisneyland’s expansion plans extend beyond its entrance and dining facilities. Among the announced developments are an expansion of Avengers Campus, with new attractions expected to open in 2028.The resort has also announced plans for a Coco-themed attraction and an Avatar experience, adding to its portfolio of immersive entertainment offerings.Together with the proposed transportation improvements and new commercial developments, these projects form part of Disney’s broader effort to expand the resort and improve the visitor experience.While the demolition of the ticket booths marks the end of a long-standing feature at Disneyland’s entrance, the wider construction programme signals a new phase in the evolution of the Anaheim resort.You use AI every day. articles.title: MS NOW issues correction after reporting Kash Patel 'landed in Russia' while he was actually in Virginia
articles.summary: The FBI mocked MS NOW after the network reported Kash Patel had landed in Russia, revealing he was actually at Liberty University in Virginia.
articles.body: The FBI accused MS NOW of incorrectly reporting FBI Director Kash Patel was in Russia on Wednesday when he was actually in Virginia, forcing the network to issue a correction. "We do have some breaking news we want to get to here on MS NOW. This is about the FBI Director, Kash Patel. MS NOW has learned that Patel has landed in Russia for a meeting scheduled to take place there," MS NOW anchor Peter Alexander told viewers, citing "two people familiar with the matter." MS NOW then brought on Justice and intelligence reporter Ken Dilanian to analyze the situation. Dilanian fretted that his FBI sources were concerned because they didn’t know why Patel was in Russia and suggested the trip would "raise a lot of eyebrows," in part due to his potential hosts being the FSB, Russia's security service. JEN PSAKI MOCKS TRUMP’S NEW PRESS SECRETARY, QUESTIONS IF SHE’S A 'POTENTIALLY FAKE LAWYER' The FBI quickly eased those concerns. Shortly after MS NOW’s breaking news was announced, the FBI Rapid Response X account mocked the liberal network, noting that Patel was actually in Virginia for a law enforcement appreciation event at Liberty University. "MS Now’s ‘sources’ are ‘familiar’ with NOTHING," the FBI Rapid Response account wrote. articles.title: UK threatens visa bans for Eritrea over migrant return policy
articles.summary: The home secretary said she would not hesitate to impose measures on other countries "refusing to co-operate".
articles.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.

From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.

Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.

Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals , according to figures from the House of Commons Library.

The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment.

"Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood.

She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".

The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.

The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission.

The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.

Earlier this year, the UK threatened bans against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved.

Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.

When announcing changes to the UK's asylum system in November, Mahmood said visa penalties would be applied to countries that failed to co-operate with returns policies.

Penalties included an "emergency brake" on visas for countries with high asylum claims until they take back citizens in the UK illegally.

According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.

There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.

Of those who had been returned, less than 6,000 has been convicted of a criminal offence.

Warnke slowly backed away, hoping the bear hadn't noticed her. Fortunately, that's when our furry friend discovered the candy bucket and apparently decided chocolate was better than human. Eventually, an announcement came over the hospital intercom warning everyone that there was a bear in the building. But that didn't stop some doctors from coming out to take pictures. articles.title: What does every marathon runner need? I asked 7 pro-runners to share the products they rely on for training, race day and recovery
articles.summary: I asked 7 professional runners about their marathon essentials for training, racing and recovery. This is the gear they can’t live without, and tips for beginners.
articles.body: One of the most surprising things about running a marathon is the sheer amount of stuff you need to be as successful and comfortable as possible. In the beginning, it might seem like the right running shoes and outfit are enough. But as you start upping your mileage, you’ll likely find yourself looking for fueling, hydrating, recovery and even chafing solutions. I know from experience that the absolute best recommendations come from professional marathon runners who’ve seen it all on the 26.2-mile course, so that’s exactly who I talked to. Below, I curated a list of marathon training, race day and recovery must-haves that Olympians, running coaches and personal trainers swear by. They’re mainly helpful for beginner marathoners, but anyone about to get their Six Star Medal might find a hidden gem too. Experts also shared their words of wisdom for the race overall, and what they wish they knew sooner. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Marathon must-haves for training and race day To curate a list of marathon must-haves for training, race day and recovery, I spoke to seven running experts, including Olympians, coaches and personal trainers, who recommended products they’ve used first-hand. As an avid runner myself, I also shared my suggestions, and I gathered a few from NBC Selected staff members. NBC Selected typically doesn’t allow people who work directly with brands and retailers to recommend products they’re affiliated with, but we made an exception in this case. Everyone included in this article is a professional running expert who based their recommendations on their personal experiences and products they’ve used for marathon training, racing or recovery. I transparently disclosed affiliations when needed, and I made sure I could back up product recommendations with NBC Selected staff feedback and/or customer reviews. Apparel “When I became a marathoner, something that became super essential for me is pockets,” says Jenny Simpson, an Olympian and the chief running officer for Fleet Feet, a running gear retailer. “Once you start stretching your mileage further, you’re going to be out there for longer, and you need pockets to put things.” She especially recommends buying a sports bra with pockets because of how well it holds heavier items like phones and keys. “I find that my phone just doesn’t bounce in my sports bra pocket nearly as much as it does in leggings or shorts, and it doesn’t get as sweaty, so it’s more comfortable over the long haul,” says Simpson. Rabbit makes one of Simpson’s favorite sports bras with pockets, and Heini Tallent, a certified running coach and the owner of Elements Running Education, recommends the brand, too. The pocket is on the back of the bra in the area between your shoulder blades, so you can reach behind you while wearing it and easily slide things in and out. Its fabric is perforated so there’s constant airflow, preventing it from holding onto sweat while you’re running. The bra also has padded straps and a cooling mesh liner. While Simpson likes a sports bra with pockets, you may prefer shorts or leggings with pockets, which Rabbit also makes for men and women. Comfortable post-race clothes Old Navy SoComfy Oversized Raglan SweatshirtOld Navy Rotation Popover HoodieOld Navy High-Waisted SoComfy Wide-Leg Sweatpants Old Navy Baggy Rotation Sweatpants When you reach the finish line and stop running, your body temperature naturally decreases because your metabolism slows down and sweat quickly evaporates. You’ll notice yourself suddenly getting cold, says Simpon, which is often why you see marathoners wrapped in heat-trapping foil blankets post-race. Most races give these blankets out, but having a dry change of clothes waiting for you is even better. “It makes you feel human again,” says Simpson. There isn’t always a place to fully change, but even putting dry clothes over your sweaty clothes helps. Simpson recommends packing a change of comfortable, loose-fitting clothes in the checked bag you pick up after your race is over. I’m a big fan of Old Navy’s sweatpants and sweatshirts for this, which are available in various men’s and women’s styles. They’re cozy, just the right amount of oversized, not super pricey and often on sale — if anything goes missing, it’s not a huge loss. Accessories Almost every marathoner I talked to recommends Body Glide’s Anti-Chafe Balm as a training and race day essential. They also wished they knew to carry a stick of it with them sooner — as someone who has plenty of running-related chafing horror stories to tell, I couldn’t agree more. “When you stack up miles, fabric and skin do a fire dance, and you will not like it,” says James McMillian, the president of Tone House, a strength and conditioning athletic training facility in New York City. Body Glide’s balm puts a barrier between fabric and skin to prevent that “fire dance”, a.k.a. rubbing that’s worsened by heat, sweat and moisture, all things that are unavoidable while running. You can use the balm on any part of your body that commonly experiences chafing, and it washes right off in the shower. One hack you should know about: Put Body Glide on your feet (just not the bottoms of them) if there’s any area where your shoe or socks are rubbing, or where you feel yourself getting a blister, says Simpson. Wearing sunscreen is never optional, especially while running long distances that require being outside for hours. For even more UV protection, Simpson recommends wearing a hat. “You’re out there for so long, and it protects your skin and eyes,” she says. “It has the added bonus of keeping those flyaway hairs out of your face, too.” Sprints’ hats are Simpson’s top pick. They have ventilated fabric that keeps your head cool, a stretchy adjustable closure and a built-in sweatband. Simpson also loves that they come in so many different colors and patterns, which she says is a fun way to personalize your race-day outfit. I’ve never been a hat person, so I rely on sunglasses to keep the light out of my eyes while running. Goodr is my go-to brand, and while I own a few pairs, I reach for the Bolt G Polarized style the most. They stay on my face phenomenally well and barely move, if at all, while I’m logging miles and getting extremely sweaty. The glasses also have vents in the reflective, polarized lenses that allow for constant airflow, reducing heat and moisture buildup that often leads to fog. Plus, there’s an adjustable nose piece, letting me custom-fit them to my face. Putting these sunglasses on and knowing that I won’t have to de-fog the lenses or adjust them on my face is such a relief whether I’m on mile one or mile 22. Many major road marathons, like the New York City and Chicago Marathons, prohibit runners from carrying rear-mounted hydration reservoirs (bladders) and backpacks due to security reasons, so make sure you research the rules of the race you’re running beforehand. You’re almost always allowed to carry handheld water bottles, soft flasks, belts with water bottles and hydration vests with front-pocket water bottles, although there may be size restrictions for each specific race that you’ll need to find out about. Tallent says Nathan makes some of the best hydration packs for men and women. This one comes with two 14-ounce water bottles you can fill up before your run and refill along the route. They have extended straws that point upward toward your face, so to drink from them, you just bend your head over and sip. The vest also has lots of pockets to put your essentials, mesh panels for constant airflow and reflective details. It comes in three sizes and there’s slider cords to customize its fit. If you’re not a fan of putting your essentials in clothes that have pockets or a vest, a running belt is also an option, although it typically only holds your phone, keys and an energy gel or two. Tallent’s favorite is the SPIbelt because it doesn’t bounce as you move. Its pocket expands to be 9-by-4-by-2 inches large to slip items inside, and it zips closed to keep everything secure. The belt also has a soft, elastic band that’s adjustable between 25 to 47 inches long. Footwear and socks “You don’t think about socks until you’re miles into a run and your feet start reminding you,” says McMillian. In fact, they’re often the cause of blisters, which many people don’t realize, so choose a pair that contours to your feet and provide a little bit of cushioning, at minimum, says Simpson. They should also be made from a breathable material that prevents heat and moisture buildup, says Tallent. High quality running socks tend to be pricier than those you’d buy in bulk at a big-box retailer, but they’re worth the investment, and they cost less than a new pair of shoes. “If the shoes that you love start rubbing a little bit, you might not immediately need a new pair,” says Simpson. “The right socks can really save them for you.” I exclusively run in Feetures’ socks, which got numerous shoutouts from the marathoners I talked to. They fit a little bit tighter, so they hug your feet more, says Simpson — this makes my arches feel extra supported, and prevents the fabric from moving around and chafing, bunching up or sliding down. They’re cushioned, but not so much that they make my shoes feel tight, and they have a seamless toe to prevent rubbing as well as moisture-wicking fabric. “I don’t care how well your shoes fit and how happy you are running into the twentieth mile with them: As soon as your race is done, it’s the most liberating thing to take your shoes off,” says Simpson. “Having a pair of recovery slides to slip on after a run became an essential to me. I would get to the last mile or two of my run and I’d be looking forward to putting on my slides.” On race day, Simpson recommends putting a pair of recovery shoes in the clear bag you check and pick up after crossing the finish line — that’s where your dry change of clothes should be, too. She says Oofos is one of the go-to recovery slides among runners, which I agree with: I learned about them when I was training for my first 10K over a decade ago, and I still wear them now. After a long run, my swollen feet breathe a sign of relief as they rest on the slides’ cushioned yet supportive base, which gently cradles my arches. They’re easy to walk in, in part due to the curved outsoles, which is important on race day when the finish line, checked bag pickup and the parking lot or public transportation might be far away from each other. Fuel and hydration Your body turns carbohydrates into glucose and stores it as glycogen in your muscles and liver, and as you do physical activity like running, your body breaks down that glycogen to use as energy, according to the Mayo Clinic. Generally, after about 90 minutes of running, your body’s glycogen stores are depleted, so you have to replenish them by consuming carbohydrates — the Mayo Clinic recommends consuming about 30 to 60 grams of carbs per hour, which you can get from sports drinks, food like fruit or energy gels and chews. All that said, there’s no perfect science to fueling during (and before) long runs: Everyone’s body is different, so what it needs to stay healthy and strong across 26.2 miles is different. Sports medicine doctors, nutritionists and dieticians can help you figure out what’s best for you. Melanie Flynn, the owner of Fitness Together Melrose, recommends testing out a few marathon fueling strategies before committing to one, and says your longest training runs are the best trials for understanding what your body needs and tolerates. There’s only one rule: Once you find products and a fueling schedule that you like, keep repeating it so your body gets used to it and there aren’t any surprises on race day, says Ali Fournier, a personal trainer at Trilogy Fitness Systems. Fournier and Tallet both like Bare Performance Nutrition Go Gels for training and racing. Fournier says they taste like applesauce, and she alternates between the gels and Gatorade to keep her energy up. The gels come in single-serving packs that fit in your belt, vest or pockets, and they have 24 grams of carbs per serving. Since you sweat a lot while running long distances, you lose fluid and electrolytes like sodium and potassium, which play a role in muscle and nerve contraction, as well as creating energy, experts told me in my guide to electrolyte powder. To ensure your body has an ample supply of both when you start running, you can dissolve electrolyte powder in water and drink the fortified beverage about two hours beforehand — doing so prevents you from feeling depleted quickly. Sodium is the most important electrolyte to pay attention to while choosing a powder because you lose it at the highest rate while sweating, experts say. You can work with sports medicine doctors, nutritionists and dieticians to find the concentration that’s right for you — experts I talked to say 500 to 1,000 milligrams of sodium is usually a good range for long distance runners. One of Tallent’s favorite electrolyte powders is from Skratch Labs, which comes in a bag with a scoop so you can customize how much you add to water based on your needs. There’s 400 milligrams of sodium in each scoop, and it also has other important electrolytes like potassium and magnesium, as well as carbohydrates. You can add electrolyte powder to water bottles you carry on long training runs or during races to replenish your electrolyte and fluid supply as you sweat. But if you plan on drinking from water stations or fountains along the route, you’ll need another way to get electrolytes. Tallent and I recommend using SaltStick FastChews, which are chewable tablets made with sodium, as well as other important electrolytes like potassium, calcium and magnesium. There’s 100 milligrams of sodium in two tablets, which the brand recommends taking about every 30 minutes while running, but do what’s best for your body. I pack the Fast Chews in a plastic bag that I put in my pockets or belt, and whenever I need them, I just pop them into my mouth while running. I really like the taste of them, too, which is an added bonus. Tech “Listening to music or podcasts can help you both zone out and stay focused when the going gets tough, but race day is so special, so I recommend planning to spend at least a few miles with your ears totally dialed into the crowd,” says Simpson. “That way, you can soak up the experience of having all those people out on the street celebrating all of your hard work.” “Shokz’s open-ear headphones let you listen to music, but they’re not actually blocking your ears, so it’s safer,” says Simpson. “I don’t use any other headphones. They’re really great quality and they’re designed to wear while you’re sweating and bouncing around, so they’re just a really great solution. There’s so few things in the world that you can have both ways, and Shokz is giving us both ways: They’re letting us enjoy our music, but also be aware of our surroundings at the same time.” “Once I started paying attention to pace, heart rate, distance and how my training was progressing over time, running became much more strategic,” says McMillian. “I like data because it gives you something to correct. How you feel matters, but sometimes you feel terrible and you’re actually performing well, or you feel great and you’re doing too much. The watch lets you know.” Garmin is one of McMillian’s favorite running watch brands, and NBC Selected editorial director Lauren Swanson has worn a few of its models while training for and doing the New York City and Chicago marathons. She recommends the Forerunner 165 most of all. “While I’m sure the other watches do more, this one gave me exactly what I needed: bells and whistles without unnecessary instruments,” says Swanson. It has built-in GPS to track your pace and distance, and it can track your sleep and heart rate, too. There’s also safety features available, and the option to get personalized workout suggestions and do training programs for events like marathons. The watch’s battery lasts up to 11 days in smartwatch mode and up to 19 hours in GPS mode, according to the brand. Recovery There are lots of fancy, high tech recovery tools out there — experts and I recommend a few of our favorites below. But one of the simplest, lowest price and most portable ones that makes a difference is a lacrosse ball, which Fournier and Flynn recommend. “I encourage runners to spend a few minutes each day using one to do soft tissue work, particularly around areas that tend to get tight from running like the hip flexors, quads, IT band and calves,” says Flynn. You can look up videos on Youtube that guide you on how to use the lacrosse balls to address problem areas and relieve tension, get rid of muscle knots and loosen up your body. Looped resistance bands like these help you do physical therapy, strength, stability and mobility work at home, says Tallent, and since they’re compact, they’re easily portable, too. You can do exercises like side-steps, glute bridges and clamshells with them, for example, and learn about even more through Youtube videos. Fit Simplify’s loops come in a pack of five, each of which is a different resistance level, and you get a storage bag to keep everything in. Many of the marathoners I talked to say that while compression boots are pricey, they’re one of the best recovery tools to invest in — I feel the same way. Therabody sent me the JetBoots Prime about two years ago and I use them multiple times a week to reduce soreness, fatigue and swelling, especially after my longest run of the week. I find wearing them very relaxing, so I typically put them on before bed. Alexi Pappas, an Olympian, is a Therabody ambassador, but she was a fan of the brand before working with it. She started using compression boots as a college athlete and still swears by them, especially because she can commit to using them consistently for prehab and rehab. “I’ve learned that the best recovery products are the ones that fit into good recovery habits,” says Pappas. “I love compression because it gives me a way to actively recover while I’m doing something else, like eating dinner, answering emails or watching a movie. After really hard efforts or races, I’ll do longer sessions, and I especially prioritize them the evening after a race and over the next few days.” My other favorite Therabody product that’s Olympian- and marathoner-approved is the Theragun Mini. I use it so much that I don’t bother putting it away at home — I immediately reach for it when I have an achy or tight spot, and I give my legs a good massage after every run. Pappas also recommends using the massage gun to wake up stiff muscles before running. She travels with it, puts it in her car and throws it in her bag at all times. “My teammates I train with all have this tool, and we all love it,” says Pappas. “A recovery tool only works if you actually use it, and the portability is why this one has become such a staple for me. Also, I love that I only need to bring my phone charger to charge it.” How to pick the best running shoes for marathons Running shoes are the most essential item you need for marathon training and racing, but it seemed unfair to feature just one pair in this article — choosing your favorite is a personal decision that depends on factors like your foot type, pace goals and fit and feel preferences. In addition to recommending marathoners’ favorite running shoes, here’s some useful advice to keep in mind while shopping for them. Run in shoes that fit: “It seems obvious, but you’d be shocked by how many people have been wearing the wrong size sneaker for years,” says Simpson. She recommends getting professionally fit and, better yet, getting a full foot analysis done to make sure your shoes are appropriate for your arch, foot length and width, foot volume and heel shape, for example. “Every part of your running experience is built off the solid foundation of whether you have a well-fitting shoe or not,” says Simpson.Pay attention to how many miles you’re putting on each pair: “You’re likely to run at least 300 to 500 miles in one marathon training cycle, which is about the typical life span of a pair of running shoes — that means one pair of shoes won’t get you through all the training and race day,” says Tallent. “At the very least, plan on getting a new pair of shoes — the same ones you know and love — before race day and putting 20 to 50 miles on them so they feel broken in but still fresh.”Try rotating your sneakers while training: To stretch out how long each pair of sneakers last, buy two pairs that you alternate between depending on what type of run you’re doing. Tallent recommends getting a pair of cushioned, comfortable shoes for easy and long runs (including the actual marathon), and a faster-feeling pair for speed and agility workouts. Training, race day and recovery tips from professional marathoners In addition to their product recommendations, the marathoners I talked to had lots of other tips for beginner runners. Below, I included some of the most common ones to keep in mind. Strength training isn’t optional. “Marathon training shouldn’t just be about running more miles,” says Flynn. “Your body needs to be strong and prepared to handle the repetitive stress that comes with running long distances over the several months of training leading up to the event.” She recommends strength training two to three times a week to expose your muscles to different types of loading, especially those in the hips, glutes, hamstrings, calves, core and upper back. Over time, doing so makes your body more resilient so it can handle how much you’re demanding from it while training and racing. Doing low-impact activities like yoga, swimming and mobility work is also helpful — it gives your body a break from the repetitive motion of running while still letting you build fitness. Make recovery part of your training plan. “Recovery should be part of the training plan, not something you do only when something hurts,” says Flynn, adding that sleep is a huge component, too. Just like you schedule your runs and strength training workouts, schedule your recovery sessions so you don’t put them off or forget about them, and be strict about bedtime. And never skip an easy run, even if you think you can push yourself harder — that often leads to injuries. “Beginners often think every run is an opportunity to prove their fitness, but the marathon rewards consistency much more than heroics,” says Pappas. “The purpose of an easy run is to allow you to arrive at the important workout ready to actually do it — that’s what my Olympic coach always said.” Practice everything. You’ve probably heard the phrase “nothing new on race day,” which all of the marathoners I talked to take very seriously. Practice what you’re going to eat before the race, how you’re going to fuel during it, where you’re going to keep all your essentials on your person, what you’re going to wear, what you’re going to tell yourself if you’re struggling — literally everything. Zachary Moxham, a personal trainer at Physical Equilibrium and a run coach for New York Road Runners, also recommends visualizing race day to create a picture in your mind of what the starting line and crowds might look like, and researching where aid and fuel stations are and what you might want to get at them. Dress rehearsing in this way can help lessen some of those pre-race jitters. Consistency matters. “There are no shortcuts when it comes to building the durability and resilience that your body needs to get to the starting line feeling healthy and strong,” says Tallent. Even when you can’t or don’t want to, trust the process as you build up your foundation, learn how to run on tired legs, figure out how to fuel and find a recovery routine that works for you. “The marathon is 26.2 miles on race day, but the real marathon is the months of training beforehand, and the biggest challenge is being able to come back and train again tomorrow,” says Pappas. “The people who inspire me most aren’t necessarily the people who can push themselves the hardest on one particular day. They’re the people who can take care of themselves well enough to make consistent progress over a long period of time, and the ones who can show up everyday along the journey.” Run your race. Don’t compare yourself to other runners, and don’t try to “beat” other runners along the route, says McMillian. Focusing on yourself will push you to run the best race possible, and help you get through the hard parts. “The marathon is a very long conversation with yourself, so don’t make a decision about how your race is going based on one mile,” says Pappas. “One of the most powerful skills an athlete can develop is staying present long enough for the moment to change.” To prioritize focusing on yourself and being present, Tallent doesn’t recommend setting a time or pace goal for your first marathon. You’re in unfamiliar territory and you’re working extremely hard, so don’t put unnecessary pressure on yourself. Recognize your huge accomplishment and embrace the journey by making goals about how you want to feel when you cross the finish line or how you’ll get through tough moments instead, she says. Meet our running experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also ensure that all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and with no undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Jenny Simpson is an Olympian and the chief running officer for Fleet Feet.Ali Fournier is a personal trainer at Trilogy Fitness Systems.Zachary Moxham is personal trainer at Physical Equilibrium and a run coach for New York Road Runners.James McMillian is the president of Tone House, a strength and conditioning athletic training facility in New York City.Alexi Pappas is an Olympian and Therabody ambassador.Melanie Flynn is the owner of Fitness Together Melrose.Heini Tallent is a certified running coach and the owner of Elements Running Education. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a reporter at NBC Selected who has covered fitness for over six years. I’ve written extensively about running, including articles about women’s running shoes, carbon plate running shoes and running shoes with arch support. As an avid long distance runner who logs over 30 miles a week, I also test dozens of running-related products every year, like sneakers, leggings, sports bras, running belts, socks and fuel. To write this article, I interviewed seven running experts about their training and race day must-haves, and gathered recommendations from NBC Selected staffers. articles.title: YouTuber Matt Walsh sounds ‘grim’ warning about AI chatbots as he questions what happens when humans replace friends
articles.summary: Conservative commentator Matt Walsh has raised concerns about young people turning to artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for regular conversations and
articles.body: Conservative commentator Matt Walsh has raised concerns about young people turning to artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for regular conversations and emotional support. In a post on X on October 14, 2026, Walsh questioned what could happen if people began spending much of their day talking to AI instead of building connections with other people. His comments followed a post describing a passenger who asked ChatGPT a simple question about bringing Cava on a flight but then became deeply involved in a conversation with the chatbot.Matt Walsh Questions the Growing Bond Between Young People and AI ChatbotsWalsh shared his concerns after reposting a post from the X account @normalboy. The original post described a passenger asking ChatGPT whether he could bring Cava, a fast-casual restaurant chain, onto a flight. The passenger then became involved in a longer conversation with the chatbot.For Walsh, the incident pointed to a bigger concern about how people use AI in their daily lives. He argued that some young people already treat chatbots like friends and spend long periods talking to them.“We need to face the fact that there’s already a huge number of people, especially younger people, who talk to AI like it’s their friend and carry on near-constant conversations with it. What happens when a critical mass of people spend most of their day bonding and communicating with an inhuman algorithm controlled by a trillion-dollar tech company? Nobody knows. Most of the dystopian sci-fi writers never even envisioned a scenario this bleak. And our leaders have apparently no interest in trying to prevent any of this from happening. Really grim stuff,” Walsh wrote on X.His main concern was not simply that people were using AI tools. Instead, he questioned what might happen if people began relying on chatbots for companionship and regular conversations. He also raised concerns about the power of large technology companies that develop and control these systems.Walsh did not provide evidence showing how many young people have formed close bonds with AI chatbots. His post instead expressed concern about a possible future in which these interactions become a major part of everyday life.Matt Walsh Has Also Raised Concerns About AI Taking Jobs and Changing Creative WorkWalsh's latest comments follow earlier criticism of AI and its growing role in society. He has questioned its possible effects on jobs, human relationships, and creative industries, including film, music, and advertising.On October 8, Walsh reacted to research published by Anthropic on September 30. The report, titled What Can Robots Do?, examined the physical tasks robots could perform and the potential effect of combining robotics with large language models. The findings discussed the difference between tasks technology could perform and those it could carry out at a competitive cost.Walsh used the research to question whether technology companies should have so much influence over changes that could affect millions of workers. He argued that people had little say in how these technologies might reshape their lives.He has also criticized AI-generated entertainment. In December 2025, he spoke out against McDonald's AI-generated Christmas advertisement, questioning its artistic value. The production studio defended the project, saying human creators had spent weeks developing prompts and refining the shots.Walsh also criticized AI-generated music, arguing that computer-made songs could threaten human creativity. His objections extend beyond whether AI can produce realistic images or music. He has questioned whether technology can replace the human experiences and creative choices that give art its meaning.His October 14 post returned to another part of the debate: how AI might affect people's relationships. While chatbots can answer questions and hold conversations, Walsh questioned what could happen if people increasingly treated them as substitutes for human connection. His post raised that concern without establishing what the long-term effects of such relationships will be.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
articles.summary: Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated.
articles.body:
On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in the quiet Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.

Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.

The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.

In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".

Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.

It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.

They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.

"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."

Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception."

When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers.

A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual.

Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m.

The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!"

The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them.

This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson.

The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.

The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.

She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.

But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.

One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.

For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.

Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.

Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.

articles.title: ED seizes assets worth over Rs 2,000 crore of Reliance Power
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) Wednesday said it has seized Indian assets worth Rs 2,033 crore belonging to Reliance Power Ltd (RPL), an
articles.body: New Delhi: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) Wednesday said it has seized Indian assets worth Rs 2,033 crore belonging to Reliance Power Ltd (RPL), an entity of the Reliance Anil Ambani Group, under Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), for the alleged siphoning of assets worth an equivalent amount to tax havens of British Virgin Islands (BVI) and Cayman Islands.The attached assets include bank balances of RPL and its shareholding in Sasan Power Limited. "The Headquarter Investigation Unit has seized assets worth ₹2,032.81 crore in India belonging to RPL, which are equivalent to the foreign exchange held outside India in contravention of FEMA," ED said. ED has already attached assets worth thousands of crores of the Anil Ambani group, including his residences in Mumbai, in multiple money laundering cases involving over Rs 40,000 crore.ED said its investigation into findings of Sebi, pertaining to write-offs/provisions aggregating ₹2,101.46 crore made by RPL in its books of account, had revealed that "these write-offs were related to overseas investments and advances made to companies in the British Virgin Islands (BVI) and the Cayman Islands".In a statement released to BSE and NSE Tuesday, RPL said the ED order of seizure of assets "relates to foreign currency convertible bonds issued in 2006, i.e. 20 years ago, and the related overseas investment made in 2008, i.e. 18 years ago, in a subsidiary in Singapore with all applicable approvals. The seizure primarily pertains to the shares held by the company in its wholly owned subsidiary Sasan Power Ltd, which are already pledged in favour of Power Finance Corporation Ltd (a govt undertaking) under security arrangements for more than 10 years, as well as certain bank balances of the company".ED had conducted related searches in March and seized "several pieces of incriminating evidence", recording statements of several persons. "Investigation has revealed that Reliance Natural Resources Ltd (since merged with RPL) raised $300 million through foreign currency convertible bonds in 2006. Of this, $275 million was invested in its wholly owned Singapore subsidiary Reliance Natural Resources (Singapore) Pte Ltd (RNRL-S)."RNRL-S placed these funds on deposit with Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA, Geneva. The deposits were used as collateral for loans extended to entities incorporated in the British Virgin Islands. The investigation found that the BVI entities were controlled and managed from India by the Reliance Anil Ambani Group (RAAG) through front persons, who acted as per the group's directions," ED said.Further, the loan proceeds were utilised for varied purposes, including temporary round-tripping of funds to India through foreign entities based in Mauritius, the central agency said, adding that this was done to benefit the RAAG."The BVI entities failed to repay the loans extended by Deutsche Bank. As part of cover-up, documents were fabricated to show that RNRL-S and Indonesian subsidiaries of RPL had made advances to these BVI entities for apparently genuine business purposes. During investigation, it was found this documentation was backdated and prepared in order to project these transactions as genuine business transactions," ED said. Further investigation is in progress.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Meet Aryash Shyam, the 14-year-old Indian-American student who won a $1,000 national writing prize for a historical-fiction story set in a Philadelphia print shop on July 4, 1776
articles.summary: A 14-year-old Indian-American student from Pennsylvania has won a $1,000 national writing prize for a historical-fiction story set in a Philadelphia print
articles.body: A 14-year-old Indian-American student from Pennsylvania has won a $1,000 national writing prize for a historical-fiction story set in a Philadelphia print shop on July 4, 1776. Aryash Shyam, a ninth-grade student at Lehigh Valley Academy, was named one of four middle-school winners of the 2026 John Estey Student Writing Competition, organised by the American Writers Museum in Chicago.His winning story, The Weight of Lead, follows a young printer's apprentice working on the Declaration of Independence. Through the experience of a 13-year-old boy, Aryash explores the difference between the promise of equality in the declaration and the reality faced by people who were not given the same freedoms.The American Writers Museum has published his story as part of the competition. According to a report by The American Bazaar, the award is among several achievements Aryash has earned in writing, science and technology. His work includes research proposals related to gene editing in space, a robotic system designed to remove invasive plants and a radio programme in which he interviews scientists.Growing up in Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley, Aryash developed an interest in understanding how things worked. "I always found myself paying attention to how everyday things work," he told The American Bazaar. "I spent a lot of time reading on my own and noticing the details of the world around me, simply out of natural curiosity," he added.The award-winning story The Weight of Leadtakes readers to Philadelphia on July 4, 1776, when the United States declared its independence from Britain. Its central character, Will, is a 13-year-old apprentice helping arrange the metal letters used to print the Declaration of Independence.As Will works with the lead letters, he begins thinking about the declaration's statement that "all men are created equal". He also becomes aware of another boy whose chances of enjoying freedom are very different from his own.Through this contrast, the story examines how the idea of equality existed alongside a society in which those rights were not available to everyone.The recognition adds to Aryash's achievements in other writing competitions. All three essays he submitted to the 2026 John Locke Institute Global Essay Prize, covering economics, philosophy, and science and technology, were shortlisted.Aryash's interest in science and space Beyond historical fiction, Aryash has worked on scientific ideas involving gene editing and space research. Earlier in 2026, he received a Genes in Space Junior Scientist Award for a proposal examining whether a CRISPR-based diagnostic system could operate in microgravity.His project, titled Validating a Cell-Free CRISPR Fluorescent RNA Diagnostic in Microgravity, studies whether a freeze-dried CRISPR-Cas13 system could be activated using water and produce a fluorescent signal when specific RNA is detected.CRISPR-Cas13 is a technology that can recognise particular RNA sequences. Aryash's proposal examines whether such a system could work in the low-gravity conditions experienced during spaceflight.The idea could have applications in monitoring astronauts' health and developing diagnostic tests for locations on Earth where medical resources are limited.Aryash was among five Junior Scientist Award recipients selected from 130 submissions by students in grades seven and eight across the United States.From medical research to roboticsIn September 2026, Aryash also secured first place in the high-school category of the American National Standards Institute Student Paper Competition.His paper, Designing Out Error: How ISO 80369 Turned a Deadly Universal Connector into a Life-Saving Standard, examined how safety standards for medical tubing connectors can help prevent dangerous mistakes.The subject was connected to his experience as a surgical patient at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. His paper explained how designing connectors that cannot fit incompatible medical systems can reduce the risk of incorrect connections.Aryash has also developed GreenBeam, an artificial intelligence-powered robotic system intended to identify and remove invasive plants without routinely using chemical herbicides."I kept coming back to a problem that seemed solvable," he said. "Invasive plant species, plants that spread aggressively outside their native range, are typically removed using chemical herbicides that can damage surrounding ecosystems. I wanted to find a better way."GreenBeam combines computer vision, which allows software to recognise plants through images, with a precision laser designed to target unwanted plants.Aryash developed the system using Python and trained it with plant images. The project earned him Pennsylvania State Merit recognition in the 2025 3M Young Scientist Challenge.Aryash also hosts a science radio programmeAryash's interest in science extends to explaining research to others. He hosts Teen Scientist, a monthly programme on WDIY 88.1 FM, Lehigh Valley Public Radio, where he interviews researchers working in artificial intelligence, biotechnology, mathematics, space and climate innovation.He has also produced Editing Humanity: A CRISPR Conundrum, a documentary exploring the science and ethical questions surrounding gene editing.Another of his initiatives is RacingGecko, a STEM-learning platform intended to help younger students understand mathematics, coding and artificial intelligence."I believe students learn better from peers who remember what it felt like to not understand something yet," Aryash said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Australian homeowner said bamboo from next door spread beneath his fence and blocked his sewer; court finds a future damage risk, orders staged removal and A$6,253.50 toward treatment and repairs
articles.summary: An Australian homeowner’s long-running dispute over invasive bamboo has ended with a court order for coordinated removal and a payment of A$6,253.50
articles.body: An Australian homeowner’s long-running dispute over invasive bamboo has ended with a court order for coordinated removal and a payment of A$6,253.50 toward treatment and likely repairs. In Wines v Homes NSW, the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales found that bamboo growing principally on a neighbouring property had spread beneath the boundary fence, previously blocked the homeowner’s terracotta sewer line, and was likely to cause further blockage and fence problems. Case Law Wire reports that Acting Commissioner Austin delivered the decision on September 29, 2026.The case is a useful reminder that garden plants can become a serious legal and financial issue when their roots cross property boundaries. While the court did not accept every claim made by the homeowner, it found enough evidence of actual and likely damage to order practical remedial action rather than leaving the problem to continue. Read more details about this case from Case Law Wire's report here:What the homeowner allegedHenry Wines and Homes NSW owned neighbouring properties on Rymill Road in Tregear, New South Wales. Wines applied under Part 2 of the Trees (Disputes Between Neighbours) Act 2006 (NSW), alleging that running bamboo originating mainly on Homes NSW’s land had spread beneath the shared boundary fence and onto his property.He said the bamboo had blocked a terracotta sewer line in 2024, damaged or displaced his Colorbond fence, reduced his use of the backyard, and created a future risk to his dwelling. He asked the court for removal and eradication works, repairs, reimbursement, access arrangements, and payment of his filing fee.The dispute centred on running bamboo, a plant known for spreading through underground rhizomes rather than staying neatly contained in one garden. Once established, it can travel beneath fences and reappear on neighbouring land, making removal difficult unless both sides address the root system.What the court foundActing Commissioner Austin granted the application in part. The court accepted that the bamboo had previously blocked Wines’ sewer pipe and was likely to cause further blockages in future. It also found that regrowth was likely to place pressure on the fence and cause it to become misaligned.Those findings were enough to engage the court’s jurisdiction under section 10(2)(a) of the Act, which allows orders where a tree on neighbouring land has caused, or is likely soon to cause, damage to property. The decision shows that bamboo can be treated as a “tree” for the purposes of the legislation when it creates a qualifying risk.However, the court did not find that the visible dents in the fence had been caused by the bamboo. It also rejected the claim that structural damage to the dwelling was likely in the near future, and it held that reduced enjoyment of the backyard was not “damage to property” under the limited statutory framework.Why the A$3,500 plumbing claim failedOne of the more significant parts of the ruling involved Wines’ request for A$3,500 to reimburse plumbing work carried out in 2024. The court refused that claim because Homes NSW had not been notified of the problem until April 2026. The court also found that Homes NSW had not contributed to the pipe damage or degradation through an act or omission. Thus, the court found that bamboo had blocked the sewer, but the neighbor could not be held liable for costs incurred years earlier because of the lack of timely notice.This section of the decision is about early recording of plant damage. Homeowners who discover roots, blockages, fence movement, or other boundary issues may strengthen their position by notifying the neighbouring owner promptly, keeping invoices and photographs, and seeking expert advice before carrying out major repairs.Staged removal and coordinated treatmentRather than ordering a single quick fix, the court approved a staged treatment and removal plan. Homes NSW was ordered to provide contractor details and begin specified works within 60 days of the decision. Wines was required to engage the contractor for coordinated treatment on his own property. That cooperative approach reflects the practical reality of bamboo removal: if the underground root system remains active on either side of the fence, regrowth can continue and the problem may return. The court did not require the root-barrier proposal that had been suggested. Instead, it focused on a staged programme capable of treating the bamboo across both properties over an extended period.The A$6,253.50 paymentHomes NSW was ordered to pay A$6,253.50 within 28 days. The payment is for previous bamboo treatment costs, and likely remedial costs, due to the situation. That was less than the full compensation Wines was seeking, but a significant contribution to the problem nonetheless. The court’s approach balanced the proven risk of future damage against the limits of what could be established about past losses. The ruling also makes clear that a court may order forward-looking action even where not every alleged past consequence has been proved. Preventing recurring sewer blockages and fence displacement was treated as a practical priority.Why this case mattersThe decision illustrates how narrowly neighbour-tree laws can operate in New South Wales. A homeowner cannot rely only on inconvenience or reduced enjoyment of their garden; they must show actual property damage or a qualifying likelihood of damage in the near future. At the same time, the case confirms that invasive bamboo can support a legal claim when it causes or threatens concrete harm. Evidence of pipe blockage and likely fence displacement was sufficient, even though some other allegations were not accepted. For homeowners, the case is a warning to take fast-spreading plants seriously. Bamboo may look attractive as a privacy screen, but running varieties can spread underground, damage drainage systems, and create expensive disputes between neighbours.A practical lesson for neighboursThe court’s order for coordinated treatment recognises that boundary disputes often require cooperation rather than blame alone. Because bamboo roots do not respect fences, successful removal may depend on both property owners allowing access and treating the plant at the same time.The case also shows why early communication matters. Had Homes NSW been aware of the sewer blockage in 2024 sooner, the outcome of reimbursement may have been different. Timely notice gives the other party an opportunity to inspect the issue, obtain advice, and respond before costs escalate.The answer is for anybody with a similar problem to keep records, get a professional assessment and seek a remedy that is focused on preventing further damage. In this case, the court chose a staged and coordinated solution designed to stop the bamboo from returning and causing new harm.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Finance minister Sitharaman rips into Akhilesh's barb on IDBI Bank sale
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party neta Akhilesh Yadav's swipe at govt over its approval for the sale of IDBI Bank drew a sharp retort from finance minister
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party neta Akhilesh Yadav's swipe at govt over its approval for the sale of IDBI Bank drew a sharp retort from finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman, who reminded him of the state of "ruin" public sector banks were left in by the previous UPA govt before they were revived by the Narendra Modi govt."Only the govt is left to be sold. It seems the BJP govt has decided to sell everything through 'season end sale' as its own shop is closing down," Akhilesh, a Congress ally, said following the Union Cabinet's nod for the bank's sale.Hitting back, Sitharaman said, "The UPA received support from your party starting in 2004. The UPA left banks in a pathetic condition. It is strange that you are talking about banks now and didn't question your allies then!""Allies now in the INDI Alliance ruined public sector banks through 'phone banking' and 'crony capitalism'. During the tenure of the UPA govt- backed by your party - IDBI Bank itself extended loans to individuals from whom recovering both the principal and the interest is an exercise we are undertaking," she said.It is the BJP-headed NDA govt under Modi that revitalised the entire banking system, including IDBI Bank, through transparent policies and the infusion of capital, she added."Now that the banks are in a strong position, you are feigning sympathy," she told the former UP CM.The 'phone banking' jibe was coined by BJP to point to how banks loaned huge sums under questionable circumstances to business houses at the prodding of certain politicians, creating a massive burden of NPAs and leading to what came to be known as the "twin balance sheet problem", and hampering growth.The Modi govt has often highlighted the record profits public sector banks have notched due to its reforms.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: India is working to develop relations with China once again, provided continuity in the engagement is warranted, geopolitical situation does not deteriorate and a fair deal is ensured, said commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal Wednesday, adding that the "last word" on this journey is not yet scripted."...I think we had some concerns in the past. We are working to develop the relations with China once again," said Goyal in response to a query whether China can be a part of joint ventures in critical sectors at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum. China is the second-largest trading partner for India, with bilateral trade rising nearly 8% in 2025-26 to $128 billion. Goyal also said ties between India and US remain "substantive" and "very consequential" for the world, which are poised to get better, irrespective of any changes in political thinking in both the countries.
